source.title: WorldToken: Time-First Sequence Modeling for Robotic Imitation Learning
source.authors: Chunkai Yang; An-Dong Yang; Di Huang; Chao Gao; Gu-Yue Zhou

record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-related outcomes in robotic imitation learning, a different training regime from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study measures holdout action RMSE and closed-loop success while varying demonstration count and model capacity. It does not measure language-model cross-entropy, scaling with training tokens or compute, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. BC-Transformer and π0.5 comparisons are contextual baselines, not scaling results for the claim.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws of held-out action RMSE against demonstration count for a Transformer imitation policy on RoboCasa. It also tracks closed-loop success rate (SR) against data, capacity and RMSE. This tests the claim's form in a non-text training regime (V5) and the link between loss and task performance (V6). It does not test LM pretraining loss, compute, extrapolation or allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report that holdout action RMSE is well described by power laws in demonstration count, and that SR improves consistently with more data. Gains from added capacity are limited beyond N3, possibly by data diversity. RMSE and SR broadly agree (ρ=-0.98) but can diverge, e.g. under context changes. Conclusions are limited to this policy family in the tested range.
record.recipe_differences: Robotic imitation-policy experiments using holdout action RMSE rather than language-model cross-entropy; varies demonstration count and model capacity, not language-model training tokens or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted data-scaling exponent varies with model capacity (0.151–0.211). The relative benefit of capacity increases with data for N1-to-N3, but further N4/N5 gains are inconsistent. Fits use means over two seeds and unweighted ordinary least squares in log space over five data sizes.
record.problems: Scaling results cover one robotic simulation benchmark and one policy family. Fits use five data sizes and two training seeds; capacity benefits are not consistent at the largest sizes. Closed-loop success evaluations use repeated fixed-seed runs, which the paper says measure repeatability rather than uncertainty over independently sampled environments. Action RMSE and task success measure different outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed seed-specific RMSE and success-rate values across all 25 capacity-by-data configurations are in Table 1 and Appendix C.1/Table 10; the record instead keeps the reported fit summaries and aggregate data-scaling results. The local BC-Transformer and reported π0.5 comparisons are not scaling results for the claim.

untested.parts: No LM held-out pretraining loss and no compute or token sweep.
No test of extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters versus data.
Depth and width co-vary across N1–N5. There is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Data range is under two orders of magnitude (50–2900 demos) with five points. No compute scaling, no repeated-data or transfer regimes, and no image/video pretraining.
No variation of parameter counting, schedule, fitting method, or comparison of published laws.

missing.what: Sweep-level Spearman correlation between holdout RMSE and SR, ρ = -0.980 across 50 policies. Also, all 40 adjacent-data comparisons show both lower RMSE and higher SR.
Per-configuration RMSE showing N5 above N3/N4 at D300–D2900 (e.g. D1000: N3 0.099/0.101 vs N5 0.109/0.108). This is the numerical basis for the non-monotone parameter scaling.

record.verdict_notes: The fits_no_version entry was moved into V6 (rows R10–R11), since it concerns whether task performance tracks loss. V7 links were removed from R1–R5: a data exponent that varies with capacity is what a joint N–D law predicts when model size bottlenecks. RMSE is an imitation error on expert crops, not the training (diffusion) loss. The data range spans about 1.8 decades with 5 points and 2 seeds.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss or power-law sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute-budget allocation or compute-optimal parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

Tests demonstration-data scaling for robotic imitation using action RMSE, not pretraining loss; does not test image/video pretraining, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer, or scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Tests closed-loop robotic task success as demonstration count and model capacity vary; does not test language-model downstream tasks or prediction from language-model pretraining loss.

Shows exponents vary by model capacity and scaling benefits depend on data, but does not vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, datasets, or fitting methods; does not compare published laws or show a curve bending away from a power law.

rows.measure: Effect of increasing capacity on holdout action RMSE
rows.value: Relative RMSE improvement from N1 to N3 increases with dataset size; further increases to N4 and N5 yield no consistent reduction.
rows.note: The result indicates that capacity benefits depend on available training data.

relationships.condition: RoboCasa imitation policies, holdout action RMSE vs demonstrations D50–D2900, each capacity N1–N5
relationships.reason: RMSE fits D^-α with α 0.151–0.211 and log–log R2 0.990–0.999. It falls 47–57% over the range (R1–R6).
relationships.display_finding: Held-out action RMSE followed demonstration power laws with exponents 0.151–0.211 and log-log R² = 0.990–0.999, decreasing 47–57% across the tested range.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: RoboCasa imitation policies, holdout action RMSE vs demonstrations D50–D2900, each capacity N1–N5
source_check.reason: R1–R6 match the reported data-scaling fits: exponents 0.151–0.211, log–log R² 0.990–0.999 and RMSE reductions of 47.0–56.8%.

relationships.condition: Scaling model capacity N3→N4→N5 (219M–1.49B) at fixed data
relationships.reason: RMSE stops falling beyond N3, and N5 is worse than N3 at D≥300. Parameter scaling therefore does not follow a power law in this range (R8).
relationships.display_finding: RMSE stopped decreasing beyond the 219M model, and the 1.49B model performed worse when D≥300.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Scaling model capacity N3→N4→N5 (219M–1.49B) at fixed data
source_check.reason: R8 shows mixed capacity benefits across data settings, qualifying extension of the data-scaling result to parameter scaling. The precise result is no consistent improvement beyond N3; N5 improves at D50 but is worse than N3 at D300–D2900.

relationships.condition: Closed-loop RoboCasa success vs training-data size, all five capacities
relationships.reason: SR rises 32.7–39.3 pp from D50 to D2900 (R7). The text also reports Spearman ρ=-0.980 between RMSE and SR across 50 policies (not in rows).
relationships.display_finding: Success rises by 32.7–39.3 percentage points across the data sweep, while RMSE and success correlate at Spearman ρ=−0.980 across 50 policies.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Closed-loop RoboCasa success vs training-data size, all five capacities
source_check.reason: R7 reports 32.7–39.3 percentage-point success gains. Appendix G.1 reports improvement in both metrics for all 40 adjacent-data comparisons; Figure 7 reports descriptive Spearman ρ = −0.980 across 50 policies.

relationships.condition: Capacity comparisons, and context-length variants at D300 with N3
relationships.reason: Larger models' RMSE advantage does not carry over to SR (R9). Lower RMSE at C=10 than C=5 comes with lower SR (R10–R11).
relationships.display_finding: Larger models' RMSE advantage did not carry over to success rate, and increasing context from C=5 to C=10 reduced both RMSE and success rate.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Capacity comparisons, and context-length variants at D300 with N3
source_check.reason: R9 qualifies how capacity-related action-fitting gains translate to task success. R10–R11 show a local RMSE–success divergence under context-specific evaluation protocols, limiting the general sweep-level association.

relation.reason: Its own capacity/data sweep fits power laws and measures whether closed-loop performance tracks scale and action error.

tranche.reason: The study tests scaling relationships in a new setting: robotic imitation learning, using demonstration count, action RMSE and closed-loop success.

source_check.notes: D denotes demonstrations per task; the fits use five in-range means, with no larger-run extrapolation test. Context variants use context-specific RMSE crops; repeated-rollout SD measures fixed-seed repeatability, not uncertainty over independently sampled environments.

statements.correction: N3→N4/N5: no consistent RMSE reduction across dataset sizes. D50 N3 RMSE: 0.195/0.194; N5: 0.189/0.186, for the two training seeds. N5 RMSE exceeds N3 at D300, D1000 and D2900. Source: Section 4.2; Table 1.
statements.problem: Saying RMSE stops improving beyond N3 overstates the result across data sizes; the paper reports no consistent reduction, and N5 improves over N3 at D50.
